chunks: From him, from Ibn Faddal, from Yunus, from Abu Maryam, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): The camel that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) passed by was a dead animal (beast of burden), and he said, 'What harm would it have done its owners if they had benefited from its hide?' He said, so Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said, 'It was not a dead animal, O Abu Maryam, but it was emaciated, so its owners slaughtered it and threw it away, and the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'It was incumbent upon its owners if they had benefited from its hide.''

key_terms.اَلسَّخْلَةُ: The camel (or young camel), specifically referring to the animal in question.
key_terms.مَيْتَةٌ: Dead animal (beast of burden), referring to an animal that died without being slaughtered.

ai.seo_question: Is an emaciated animal that was slaughtered by its owners considered halal or haram?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia juristic principle that an animal discarded by its owner is considered *mubah* (permissible) rather than *maytah* (impure carcass), provided it is slaughtered. Imam al-Sadiq clarifies that the Prophet’s remark regarding the hide confirms the validity of the slaughter, distinguishing this state from a true dead animal that died of natural causes. This distinction is crucial for determining the purity of the meat and its hide in Islamic dietary law.
